location: Pacific Ocean, 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California
the_unresolved_thing: The lubrication interval on the jackscrew was extended four times between 1987 and 1996 and the FAA approved every extension. No investigation established what data the FAA believed it was reviewing.

structural_test.why: Approval chain, not failure sequence. Four approvals, no supporting data on the record.

commonly_wrong.record: The jackscrew survived. The acme nut riding on it lost its threads; roughly 90% had already worn away.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: Confusing the shaft with the nut misattributes the failure mode entirely.

commonly_wrong.record: The interval itself was extended, repeatedly and with approval. The NTSB named the extensions and the FAA's approval of them as contributing causes.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: It was not an individual lapse. It was an authorised schedule.

commonly_wrong.record: In 1997 a lead mechanic found the end play at its 0.040 inch limit and ordered the assembly replaced. The aircraft returned to service days later with it installed.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: There is a documented flag on this exact assembly, years early.

slides.text: Everyone aboard Alaska Airlines Flight 261 died in the Pacific, 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, on 31 January 2000.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: The jackscrew never broke.
slides.text: The shaft survived the impact. What failed was the acme nut riding on it. Roughly 90% of its threads had already worn away before the aircraft ever left the gate.

slides.label: The barrier
slides.headline: One screw. No backup.
slides.text: The MD-80 horizontal stabilizer is driven by a single jackscrew. Lose the acme nut threads and you lose pitch control entirely. There is no second system.

slides.label: The document
slides.headline: 0.040 inches. Replace it.
slides.text: In 1997 a lead mechanic measured the end play at its maximum allowable limit and ordered the assembly replaced. The aircraft was back in service within days, same part fitted.

slides.label: The interval
slides.headline: 500 hours became 2,550.
slides.text: The lubrication interval was extended four times between 1987 and 1996. By July 1996 it stood at eight calendar months. The end play inspection interval was stretched as well.

slides.label: Who approved it
slides.headline: The FAA signed all four.
slides.text: Every extension was authorised. The NTSB found no supporting data was offered for any of them, and named both the extensions and their approval as contributing causes.
83 passengers and 5 crew. There were no survivors.

slides.label: Unresolved
slides.headline: Reviewing what, exactly?
slides.text: No investigation ever established what data the FAA believed it was assessing when it approved four consecutive extensions to the interval that kept this assembly alive.

source_line: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-02/01, 10 December 2002; NTSB Docket DCA00MA023.
caption:
The jackscrew on Alaska 261 never broke. The nut riding on it lost its threads.

The lubrication interval for that assembly started at 500 flight hours. By 1996 it had been extended four times, to roughly 2,550. The FAA approved every extension and the NTSB found no supporting data was offered for any of them.

Source: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report AAR-02/01; NTSB Docket DCA00MA023.

slides.text: Eleven officers and seven bystanders were hit outside a Bank of America in North Hollywood on 28 February 1997. Every one of them lived.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: They weren't armor-piercing rounds.
slides.text: The press said armor-piercing. The record says standard 7.62x39 and 5.56 rifle ammunition. What beat the officers was the gap between a handgun and a rifle, not exotic bullets.

slides.headline: A 9mm against a rifle plate.
slides.text: Patrol officers carried 9mm sidearms, .38 revolvers and shotguns. The robbers wore homemade Type III-A armor with a trauma plate. Nothing the officers carried went through it.

slides.label: The document
slides.headline: Buckshot only.

slides.label: The improvisation
slides.headline: They borrowed the rifles.
slides.text: Officers drove to a gun shop three blocks away and commandeered AR-15s off the rack. A department of nine thousand officers armed itself mid-incident from a retail shelf.

case_name: Apollo 13 Service Module Oxygen Tank 2 Explosion
location: Space, 205,000 miles from Earth en route to Moon
coordinates: N/A (deep space, approx. 205,000 miles from Earth)
the_number: Oxygen Tank 2, serial number 10024X-TA0009, exploded at 55 hours 55 minutes into flight
the_unresolved_thing: Who was accountable for enforcing the thermostat voltage change across the contractor chain, what documentation was supposed to flow the requirement down from ASPO through North American Rockwell to Beech Aircraft, and why no testing procedure ever required the switches to cycle under load at 65V before the tanks were qualified for flight.

structural_test.why: The Cortright Commission identified a definite approval chain failure: NASA's Apollo Spacecraft Program Office (ASPO) directed that Kennedy Space Center ground support equipment (GSE) supply 65V DC to oxygen tank heaters. North American Rockwell (NR), the prime contractor, was responsible for flowing this change down to subcontractors such as Beech Aircraft Corporation. North American Aviation and ASPO ordered Beech to fit a 65-volt thermostat switch in all Block 2 tanks, but Beech did not do it and the program office did not follow up. The discrepancy was not detected by NASA, NR, or Beech in their review of documentation, nor did tests identify the incompatibility, since neither qualification nor acceptance testing required switch cycling under load. This is not a failure-sequence timing dispute; it is an unresolved authorization gap: no investigation established what data the three parties believed they were reviewing or why the change order was never enforced.

commonly_wrong.claim: The tank failure was caused by a simple oversight in the wiring.
commonly_wrong.record: The switch was never classified 'flight-critical' because it only operated during ground procedures. NR issued a blanket requirement for 65V compatibility but did not explicitly list the internal thermostatic switch as needing a part change, and Beech continued installing the original 28V switches per the drawings on file.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The failure was not a single missed part. It was a requirement that was issued, never flowed down, and never checked at three separate points in the chain.

commonly_wrong.claim: Engineers saw the tank overheating during the March 1970 ground test.
commonly_wrong.record: The temperature gauge for the heater could only record up to 85 degrees F. Most of the individuals involved in the detanking discussion knew nothing of the extended heater and fan operation, so the off-nominal heating was invisible to them at the time.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The instrument that should have caught the fault physically could not read high enough to show it.

commonly_wrong.claim: The thermostat was upgraded to 65 volts along with the rest of the tank hardware.
commonly_wrong.record: The 1965 modification touched virtually every component except the thermostatic safety switches inside the oxygen tank heaters. Beech kept building tanks with the original 28V switch for four years.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: It is the one component the change order was actually about, and it is the one component the change never reached.

could_not_verify.item: Whether any pre-1970 safety recommendation specifically addressed the thermostat voltage rating gap before Apollo 13.
could_not_verify.note: No primary source located confirming or denying a prior recommendation on this specific gap.

could_not_verify.item: Which Cortright recommendation directly led to the thermostat upgrade and whether it was ever marked 'closed unacceptable' or revisited.
could_not_verify.note: Recommendation tracking status not confirmed in sources retrieved.

could_not_verify.item: Whether North American Rockwell documented the initial change order directing Beech to upgrade the thermostat, and if so, where it was archived.
could_not_verify.note: No archival record of the specific change order document was located.

location: Atlantic Ocean, off Cape Canaveral, Florida
agency: Rogers Commission (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident)
the_unresolved_thing: NASA and Thiokol continued operating the field joint design and approving launches despite certification programs that neither agency understood to be adequate, and no post-Commission investigation ever settled what either agency believed it was actually reviewing when it certified the O-ring seal as flight-ready.

structural_test.why: The Rogers Commission concluded the O-ring flaw was known to NASA managers as early as 1977, and both NASA and Thiokol accepted the joint's unsuitability as a baseline rather than demanding redesign. The open question is not the failure sequence, it is why the certification process kept permitting flight of a component both agencies knew was eroding, and on what data.

commonly_wrong.claim: The night before the launch, Thiokol engineers warned NASA that the O-rings were dangerous, and NASA ignored them.
commonly_wrong.record: Thiokol management initially recommended against launching below 53 degrees. After NASA personnel challenged that reasoning and Thiokol requested a recess, Thiokol management reversed its own position and recommended proceeding with the launch.
commonly_wrong.source: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 1, Ch. V-VI
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The warning did not go unheard. It was withdrawn by the same company that issued it, after NASA pushed back on the data, not the risk.

investigators_disagree.question: Did the Rogers Commission and the later Congressional investigation reach different conclusions on the immediate cause?
investigators_disagree.position_a: Rogers Commission: failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right solid rocket motor, due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to temperature, dynamic loading, and other factors.
investigators_disagree.position_b: House Committee on Science and Technology: affirms the same joint design flaw and finds neither NASA nor Thiokol fully understood the joint's operation prior to the accident.
investigators_disagree.status: No disagreement between the two bodies on the physical cause. The disagreement that never got resolved is upstream of both reports, in the certification and waiver process itself.

could_not_verify.item: The exact start time of the January 27 teleconference between Thiokol and NASA.
could_not_verify.note: Secondary sources cite 8:45 p.m. but this could not be confirmed against the primary Rogers Commission transcript.

could_not_verify.item: The statement attributed to NASA's Lawrence Mulloy: 'My God Thiokol, when do you want me to launch? Next April?'
could_not_verify.note: Appears only in secondary analysis, not in Rogers Commission testimony or hearing transcripts.

could_not_verify.item: The specific schedule pressure NASA managers cited to reverse Thiokol's no-launch position during the recess.
could_not_verify.note: The Commission describes generalized 'institutional pressure' but does not attribute a specific statement to a specific manager during the recess.

slides.headline: 73 seconds
slides.text: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members.
slides.visual: Black frame, white type only. No launch photo on this slide.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: Thiokol didn't warn NASA. They reversed.
slides.text: The night before launch, Thiokol's engineers recommended against flying below 53 degrees. After NASA challenged the data and Thiokol took a recess, Thiokol management reversed that recommendation and cleared the launch.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. V text excerpt, cropped tight.

slides.label: The safeguard that existed
slides.headline: 23 launches. Minimum temp: 53°F.
slides.text: Every prior shuttle flight had launched above 53 degrees Fahrenheit, the coldest data point Thiokol had for O-ring performance. Challenger launched at 36 degrees, 15 degrees below any flight on record.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI temperature chart, document excerpt only.

slides.label: What NASA knew, and when
slides.headline: 1977: the joint rotation problem is already on paper.
slides.text: The Commission found NASA managers were aware of O-ring erosion and joint rotation concerns as early as 1977, nine years before the accident. Launches continued.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. IV, document excerpt.

slides.label: Investigators disagree
slides.headline: Same joint. Same flaw. No agreement on why it was allowed.
slides.text: The Rogers Commission and the House Committee on Science and Technology both identified the same field joint design flaw. Neither report resolved how a joint with a documented erosion history kept receiving flight certification.
slides.visual: House Committee Report GPO-CRPT-99hrpt1016 cover page, document excerpt.

slides.label: The permission, not the mechanism
slides.headline: Waivers, not redesign.
slides.text: Rather than redesigning the joint after erosion was first observed, NASA and Thiokol treated each instance of O-ring erosion within a widening margin of what they considered 'acceptable risk,' a margin that expanded with each successful flight rather than contracting.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, 'acceptable risk' text excerpt.

slides.label: The recess
slides.headline: Thiokol asked for five minutes. Took thirty.
slides.text: During the January 27 teleconference, Thiokol engineers recommended against launch. NASA officials questioned the flight-readiness rationale. Thiokol requested a caucus, and returned roughly thirty minutes later with a reversed recommendation to launch.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. V, teleconference summary excerpt.

slides.label: What the record shows
slides.headline: No new data. Same data, different conclusion.
slides.text: The Commission found that no new engineering data was introduced during the recess. The same temperature and erosion data was reinterpreted to support a different outcome.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, findings text excerpt.

slides.label: What was never settled
slides.headline: No investigation ever fixed what 'flight-ready' meant.
slides.text: Both NASA's certification process and Thiokol's engineering sign-off continued for years without a shared, documented standard for what data justified clearing a known erosion defect for flight. Neither the Rogers Commission nor Congress resolved what either organization believed it was actually reviewing when it certified the joint.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, closing findings page, document excerpt only.

location: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa
the_unresolved_thing: The FAA certified the DC-10 hydraulic system on McDonnell Douglas's statement that an uncontained engine failure destroying all three hydraulic systems was extremely remote, though the design routed all three lines through the same section of the tail. When the No. 2 engine's fan disk disintegrated on July 19, 1989, titanium fragments severed all three systems in milliseconds. No investigation established what data supported the original probability calculation, or whether it was ever tested against the actual failure mode.

structural_test.why: Two fault chains stand unresolved: the adequacy of FAA review of hydraulic routing under Special Condition 25-18-WE-7, which assumed total hydraulic loss was 'extremely remote,' versus the vulnerability that was actually built in; and whether the titanium defect introduced during 1971 manufacture was ever detectable by General Electric's quality controls.

commonly_wrong.claim: The hydraulic lines should have been separated.
commonly_wrong.record: The three systems were independent in fluid, pumps, reservoirs, and control logic, but not in physical routing. All three lines passed through the same section of the tail, a design certified by the FAA on the assumption that a single engine failure would not sever all three.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The failure wasn't a lack of redundancy. It was redundancy built around a probability that turned out to be wrong.

commonly_wrong.claim: The crew had no backup systems.
commonly_wrong.record: The DC-10 carried a ram air turbine providing emergency electrical power to auxiliary pumps if engine power or primary pumps failed. It could not restore fluid pressure once all three systems had already lost fluid, a scenario excluded from the original failure analysis.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The backup worked exactly as designed. The design never accounted for the failure that occurred.

commonly_wrong.claim: The metallurgical defect was undetectable at the time.
commonly_wrong.record: The nitrogen inclusion formed during 1971 forging was smaller than a fingernail. It survived six fluorescent penetrant inspections over 17 years. NTSB's probable cause cited inadequate consideration of human factors limitations in United's inspection procedures, not the detection method itself.
commonly_wrong.source: NTSB AAR-90/06; FAA Lessons Learned, N1819U
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The defect wasn't invisible. The inspection process wasn't built to catch what a human eye could miss.

investigators_disagree.question: What was the true causal chain behind the loss of all three hydraulic systems?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB probable cause: inadequate inspection procedures at United Airlines' overhaul facility allowed the 1971 titanium defect to go undetected, leading to fan disk failure.
investigators_disagree.position_b: Post-accident engineering analysis: the initiating failure was FAA certification philosophy, which allowed a hydraulic routing design with a common-cause vulnerability to be certified on an unvalidated probability estimate.
investigators_disagree.status: NTSB's probable cause is the official record. The certification critique has never been formally adjudicated by any agency and remains outside the closed finding.

could_not_verify.item: The exact text or methodology of the McDonnell Douglas probability calculation submitted under Special Condition 25-18-WE-7.
could_not_verify.note: Referenced in post-accident engineering literature; not located as a primary FAA or NTSB exhibit in this research pass.

could_not_verify.item: Whether the FAA formally reviewed the hydraulic routing design or relied on Douglas's written assurance alone.
could_not_verify.note: Certification record on this specific review step not confirmed in NTSB AAR-90/06 as retrieved.

could_not_verify.item: Specific General Electric quality control procedures in effect at the 1971 forging that allowed the nitrogen inclusion through.
could_not_verify.note: General manufacturing background is in the FAA Lessons Learned page; process-level detail not independently verified.

could_not_verify.item: Current status (open/closed) of any NTSB recommendation specifically addressing hydraulic routing common-cause vulnerability.
could_not_verify.note: Safety recommendation letters A-90-167 through A-90-175 exist but their present disposition was not confirmed this session.

slides.headline: 112 dead. 184 survived a jet with zero hydraulics.
slides.text: United Airlines Flight 232, a DC-10, lost all three hydraulic systems over Iowa on July 19, 1989. The crew crash-landed at Sioux City using only engine thrust for control.
slides.visual: NTSB AAR-90/06 Figure 6, wreckage path diagram, full bleed

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: Independent hydraulics, one physical bottleneck
slides.text: The three systems were independent in fluid, pumps, and control logic. All three lines were also routed through the same section of the tail, a design certified by the FAA as adequate protection against loss of any single system.
slides.visual: Simple line diagram built from NTSB report text, no third-party graphics

slides.label: The safeguard that existed
slides.headline: A backup existed for engine failure
slides.text: The DC-10 carried a ram air turbine to restore electrical power to auxiliary pumps if primary pumps failed. It could not restore fluid to a system that had already lost pressure, and total loss of all three was rated extremely remote at certification.
slides.visual: Text card, NTSB AAR-90/06 excerpt on hydraulic system design

slides.label: The certification record
slides.headline: The certification word was 'improbable'
slides.text: Special Condition 25-18-WE-7 required McDonnell Douglas to show that total hydraulic loss from an uncontained engine failure was extremely remote. No formal industry standard for uncontained-engine protection existed at the time of certification.
slides.visual: Scanned excerpt, NTSB AAR-90/06, certification section

slides.label: The moment it read true
slides.headline: All three gauges read zero
slides.text: At 1516 CDT, a fan disk from the No. 2 engine disintegrated. Within seconds, the flight crew found hydraulic pressure and quantity gauges for systems one, two, and three all at zero, a condition the design had not anticipated.
slides.visual: NTSB AAR-90/06 Figure 3, in-flight photo of stabilizer and missing cowl door

slides.label: Why no one caught it
slides.headline: No rule required this protection
slides.text: At the time the DC-10 was certified in 1971, no FAA requirement or industry standard addressed uncontained engine failure as a design hazard for hydraulic systems. The redundancy built in was judged sufficient against every failure mode considered probable.

slides.headline: Two failures, one still open

case_name: Lion Air Flight 610 / Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 (Boeing 737 MAX MCAS Certification)
location: Java Sea near Jakarta, Indonesia / near Ejere, Ethiopia
agency: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure; FAA; NTSB; DOT OIG
the_unresolved_thing: The FAA's 2015 decision to delegate MCAS safety assessments to Boeing under the ODA program was never independently verified by agency documents that now exist in the public record. The DOT OIG stated in June 2020 that 'FAA did not have a complete understanding of Boeing's safety assessments performed on MCAS until after the first accident,' meaning the approval chain rested on Boeing's own representations. No safety recommendation was ever issued or closed on the delegation decision itself or the criteria used to classify MCAS as 'major' rather than 'hazardous.'

structural_test.why: Two federal bodies (House Committee, DOT OIG) and the FAA itself reached opposite conclusions on whether the agency understood what it had delegated, and the delegation criteria were never independently reconstructed. Both findings still stand.

commonly_wrong.claim: Boeing hid MCAS from pilots to avoid training requirements
commonly_wrong.record: On June 7, 2013, Boeing staff concluded internally: 'If we emphasize MCAS is a new function there may be a greater certification and training impact.' They decided to 'externally communicate it as an addition to the Speed Trim' while developing it internally as a new system. Boeing told the FAA about MCAS repeatedly during certification; it downplayed the system's scope in certification documents.
commonly_wrong.source: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure Final Report, Sept. 2020
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The distinction between a certification strategy and a hidden system changes who bears responsibility for FAA's incomplete picture, and whether existing disclosure rules were even adequate to catch it.

commonly_wrong.claim: The FAA never knew MCAS could move the plane's nose down repeatedly
commonly_wrong.record: Boeing's own System Safety Analysis, submitted to the FAA, 'underestimated the power of MCAS to move the plane's horizontal tail' and 'did not account for the system deploying multiple times.' Boeing changed MCAS design during certification, making it more powerful, and 'key people at FAA were not always told.'
commonly_wrong.source: NTSB, DOT OIG, House Committee Final Report
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The failure was not agency ignorance of a hidden fact but the FAA's acceptance of a flawed analysis it was supposed to validate independently.

commonly_wrong.claim: MCAS was approved as a single-sensor system despite known risks
commonly_wrong.record: An unnamed Boeing engineer raised concerns internally in 2015 about 'relying on a single AOA sensor.' Boeing's safety analysis classified MCAS failure as 'major,' meaning the flight crew serves as the backup, rather than requiring dual-sensor input. The FAA accepted that classification without independent review.
commonly_wrong.source: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure Final Report, Sept. 2020
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The structural gap was not the sensor count. It was who got to decide the risk category that made a single sensor acceptable.

investigators_disagree.question: Whether the FAA had adequate understanding of MCAS before the crashes
investigators_disagree.position_a: House Committee: FAA oversight was 'hampered by poor, disjointed FAA communication among the agency's own internal offices responsible for certifying new critical 737 MAX systems, including MCAS.' DOT OIG, June 2020: 'FAA did not have a complete understanding of Boeing's safety assessments performed on MCAS until after the first accident.'
investigators_disagree.position_b: FAA testimony: the agency was 'directly involved in the System Safety Review' of MCAS, cited 297 certification flight tests including MCAS testing, and called the certification process 'detailed and thorough.'
investigators_disagree.status: Still unresolved. No finding established whether documented 'involvement' without independent validation of Boeing's analysis constitutes adequate understanding.

investigators_disagree.question: Whether MCAS should have been classified as 'hazardous' rather than 'major'
investigators_disagree.position_a: A May 2019 internal FAA administrative review 'tentatively determined that senior agency officials didn't participate in or monitor crucial safety assessments,' and noted Boeing 'didn't flag the automated stall-prevention feature as a system whose malfunction or failure could cause a catastrophic event.'
investigators_disagree.position_b: The FAA later acknowledged MCAS should have been considered 'safety-critical,' but characterized this as a post-accident reassessment, not evidence the 2015 classification logic was wrong at the time.
investigators_disagree.status: Never resolved. No investigation determined what classification MCAS should have received under 2015 standards or who at the FAA was responsible for validating it before delegation.

investigators_disagree.question: Whether the failure was communication breakdown or intentional concealment
investigators_disagree.position_a: Joint Authorities Technical Review, chaired by former NTSB chairman Christopher Hart: MCAS 'evolved from a relatively benign system to a not-so-benign system without adequate knowledge by the FAA,' with 'no indication of intentional wrongdoing.'
investigators_disagree.position_b: The Department of Justice: Boeing pleaded guilty in January 2021 to conspiracy to defraud the United States, admitting it 'engaged in criminal conduct intended to deceive and mislead the Federal Aviation Administration' through 'misleading statements, half-truths, and omissions.'
investigators_disagree.status: Both findings stand. No single investigation reconciled a safety panel's finding of no intentional wrongdoing with a signed federal guilty plea to fraud.

could_not_verify.note: No public document names the specific reviewers or review dates.

location: Bligh Reef, Prince William Sound, near Valdez, Alaska
the_number: 11 million gallons (10.8 million US gallons per NTSB/Coast Guard/State of Alaska)
the_unresolved_thing: Exxon knew the tanker's RAYCAS collision-avoidance radar had been disabled for over a year, but that fact does not appear in NTSB's official probable cause statement or findings, per secondary reporting that surfaced it after the fact.

structural_test.why: This is not two standing bodies with opposite findings. It is a single agency's report that omits a documented, known equipment failure. Correction-drop material, not long-form.

commonly_wrong.claim: News coverage treats Captain Hazelwood's drinking as the cause of the spill.
commonly_wrong.record: NTSB's probable cause statement weighs the captain's alcohol impairment alongside the third mate's fatigue and failure to maneuver, Exxon's crew staffing, and the Coast Guard's failed vessel traffic monitoring, as roughly equal causal factors.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The public narrative isolates one man; the agency's own finding spreads responsibility across four separate parties.

commonly_wrong.claim: The broken radar is what caused the grounding.
commonly_wrong.record: Multiple secondary sources report Exxon knew the RAYCAS radar was disabled for over a year, but per Wikipedia's summary of the case, this factor is not presented in the official accident report.
commonly_wrong.source: Secondary reporting (Greg Palast); not confirmed in NTSB report text
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: A widely repeated claim outruns what the official record actually states.

investigators_disagree.question: What role did the disabled RAYCAS radar play in the probable cause?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB's official probable cause statement does not address the radar's condition.
investigators_disagree.position_b: Investigative reporting (Greg Palast) identifies the disabled radar as a factor that would have detected Bligh Reef.
investigators_disagree.status: Unresolved. No source confirms whether this was a deliberate omission, a secondary finding buried outside probable cause, or a genuine gap in the investigation.

investigators_disagree.question: Did Coast Guard inspections check radar maintenance compliance?
investigators_disagree.position_a: NTSB found the Coast Guard failed to maintain effective vessel traffic monitoring; GAO found Valdez tanker inspections were not being conducted and staffing had been reduced.
investigators_disagree.position_b: No source confirms whether radar operational testing was ever part of the inspection protocol.
investigators_disagree.status: Unresolved. No document in the accessible record specifies an inspection standard for onboard collision-avoidance radar in 1988-89.

could_not_verify.note: Sources describe it only as 'over a year' before the grounding.

could_not_verify.item: Whether federal regulation required collision-avoidance radar maintenance certification in 1988-89
could_not_verify.note: No confirming source found.

could_not_verify.item: Whether Coast Guard inspections included radar operational testing
could_not_verify.note: GAO report cites reduced staffing and skipped inspections but does not detail checklist contents.

caption:
11 million gallons.

That's what spilled when the Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, March 24, 1989. NTSB's official probable cause names four causal factors, and a radar that had been broken for over a year isn't one of them.

Source: NTSB Marine Accident Report MAR-90/04.
60.8400°N, 146.8625°W
x_post: NTSB's official probable cause for the Exxon Valdez grounding names four factors: captain impairment, third mate fatigue, Exxon's crew staffing, and Coast Guard's failed vessel traffic service. A radar that had been broken for over a year isn't one of them.

hook_alternates.hook: NTSB's report blames the captain. It doesn't mention the radar that had been broken for a year.
Zero deaths. Eleven million gallons. Four causal factors in the official report, and the broken radar is not one of them.
